new_statements.quote: Natqgu, like most Oceanic languages, exhibits stress on the penultimate mora of a syllable. Single morphemes have been identified with from one to six syllables. Most roots are comprised of one, two or three syllables. Primary stress remains penultimate in multisyllabic complex words. The placement of secondary stress correlates with the basic foot type found in Natügu. Beyond one-syllable words the foot type is a syllabic trochee. That is, feet are left headed and quantity insensitive.
new_statements.citation: Boerger, Brenda H. 2022. A Grammar Sketch of Natqgu [ntu]: An Oceanic language of Santa Cruz, Solomon Islands. Port Moresby: Linguistic Society of Papua New Guinea (LLM 'Texts in the Indigenous Languages of the Pacific' 2020-2023 collection). 71 pp.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Stress, p. 4 (printed page 4; PDF page 5 area, between page footers 3 and 4); supporting example §2.5 Rule 4, p. 7
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: the full passage is present verbatim in the text of ( lines 177-183, heading "2.3 Stress"): "Natqgu, like most Oceanic languages, exhibits stress on the penultimate mora of a syllable. Single morphemes have been identified with from one to six syllables. Most roots are comprised of one, two or three syllables. Primary stress remains penultimate in multisyllabic complex words. The placement of secondary stress correlates with the basic foot type found in Natügu. Beyond one-syllable words the foot type is a syllabic trochee. That is, feet are left headed and quantity insensitive." Only the locator is slightly off: per-page extracted text shows page footers equal PDF page numbers, so §2…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable (the author writes 'penultimate mora of a syllable', evidently meaning of the word) and stays penultimate in morphologically complex words; feet are left-headed, quantity-insensitive syllabic trochees, so secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables leftward. Stress is assigned before fast-speech deletion of word-final q [y], so a surface form such as [vztrpʰ] 'come in' can sound final-stressed (p. 7).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated in principle only: secondary stress follows the syllabic-trochee foot type (left-headed, quantity-insensitive); no examples given.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated as lexical exceptions. §2.1 (p. 3): a second vowel of a VV sequence that must bear stress is syllabified separately (na-iklö [na.'i.kʰlö]); §2.5 Rule 4 (p. 7): apparent surface final stress after word-final q-deletion. Older Wurm 1969: 60 / 1970: 477 / 1976: 643 n. 6 said stress only partly predictable and 'may be phonemic'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (single morphemes and multisyllabic complex words, i.e. the verb complex); no phrase-level statement; impressionistic, no instrumental data; Natügu of the Graciosa Bay area (Bznwz village).
new_statements.identity_note: natu1249 is not a language: it is Glottolog's Bookkeeping entry for the retired ISO 639-3 code [stc] "Santa Cruz", split on 2009-01-16 (CR 2008-070, into Natügu [ntu] = natu1246 (Northern Santa Cruz, Wurm's 'Malo') and Nalögo [nlz] = nalo1235 (Southern Santa Cruz). The statement quoted is the Natügu one (natu1246), which already has a WORLD_RESULTS entry with this same quote; Nalögo's stress is described separately by Alfarano 2021 §2.5 (weight-sensitive, mora-based) in the nalo1235 catalog folder. Recommend reclassification natu1249 -> natu1246 (with nalo1235 as the second referent) rather than cataloguing it as its own row.

new_statements.quote: L'accent : L'accent peut frapper n'importe quelle syllabe du mot. Ainsi : nény (vent), møréa (village), dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy (la nourriture, la chose qui se mange) : c'est dans ce dernier cas l'article qui est accentué : ŋy (manger, terme poli) précédé de l'article nǿ-ŋy (le manger), da reçoit un accent secondaire. Dans tœ-mámi (le volcan), c'est l'élément lexical qui est mis en valeur par rapport à l'outil grammatical, dont il est d'ailleurs inséparable.
new_statements.translation: Stress: Stress can fall on any syllable of the word. Thus: nény 'wind', møréa 'village', dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy 'food, the thing that is eaten': in this last case it is the article that is stressed: ŋy 'to eat (polite term)' preceded by the article, nǿ-ŋy 'the eating'; da receives a secondary stress. In tœ-mámi 'the volcano' it is the lexical element that is given prominence relative to the grammatical tool, from which it is moreover inseparable.
new_statements.citation: de la Fontinelle, Jacqueline. 1974. Notes sur le dialecte de Néo, île de Malo ou plus exactement Tö-mótu Néo, archipel des Santa-Cruz. Journal de la Société des Océanistes 30(45): 283-299.
new_statements.locator: §II (phonology), paragraph 'L'accent', p. 288 (last paragraph) continuing onto p. 289 (first paragraph); supporting remarks on p. 285 ('deux types accentuels : CW et 'CW'), p. 288 ('Les voyelles longues': length = accent on the first mora of a sequence of identical vowels), pp. 293-294 (accent marks the classifier/root boundary; accented vs unaccented classifiers; torô, tomuna 'accentués sur la seconde syllabe'), p. 296 (wordlist convention: apostrophe before the stressed syllable)

new_statements.relation_note: The existing statement of record (Boerger 2022, Grammar Sketch of Natqgu, §2.3) says primary stress is fixed on the penultimate (syllabic trochee, quantity-insensitive). De la Fontinelle 1974 states explicitly that stress may fall on any syllable, i.e. lexically/morphologically placed, not fixed — a different type. The disagreement is partly dialectal and partly analytic: she describes the Néo dialect of Tömotu Neo (Malo island) from a few days with one expatriate informant in 1972, and her examples and wordlist are overwhelmingly penultimate; the free-stress claim rests on the accented/unaccented status of grammatical prefixes rather than on demonstrated minimal pairs. It is closer to Wurm…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The author states that stress (accent) may fall on any syllable of the word; its position is tied to morphology (some articles/classifiers are accented, e.g. né-, nǿ-, others such as no-, to-, ma- are unaccented, so stress marks the boundary between grammatical tool and root, pp. 293-294), and accent contrasts are used to explain glide/vowel sequences (CW vs 'CW, p. 285) and the single long vowel lóo (stress on the first mora, p. 288). Her own cited examples (nény, møréa, dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy, tœ-mámi) and most of the stress-marked wordlist (pp. 296-299: e'sama, o'lima, na'lapû, esi'kapu, lô'paki, mi'tapû, bo'rjava, na'blôvi, daka'nalx …) are in fact penultimate, with a minority of non-penultimate items (torô final; 'esâmœ, 'etlomœ antepenultimate as scanned-read; ve'i, ma'i, nœl'vyn final).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Mentioned once: in the compound dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy the first element da 'receives a secondary stress' (reçoit un accent secondaire), p. 289; no general rule given.
new_statements.exceptions: No exceptions in the usual sense, since no fixed rule is claimed; noted specifics: classifiers/articles differ in being accented (né-/nǿ-, ni-) or unaccented (no-, to-, ma-), pp. 293-294; torô 'sprouted coconut' and tomuna 'fat' are stressed on the second syllable, p. 294; borrowed and old words with the article te-/tœ- keep root stress (tœ-pûri, te-ômo, te-môtu, tœ-kytu, tœ-klâva), p. 294.
new_statements.identity_note: de la Fontinelle 1974 describes the Néo (Neo) dialect of Tömotu Neo (Malo island), off the north coast of Santa Cruz (Nendö), from a single informant, Margaret Worek née Inaglai, interviewed for a few days in 1972 in the New Hebrides; she contrasts it with Wurm's Malo dialect on the opposite coast of the same islet. Boerger & Zimmerman 2012 (held by the project in this directory) list both Neo and Malo among the Natügu (NW) dialect groupings, so the work is about Natügu [ntu] = natu1246, within the retired [stc] scope of natu1249. natu1249 itself is not a distinct language: it is the Glottolog bookkeeping entry for the ISO code split in 2009 into Natügu and Nalögo.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement. De la Fontinelle 1974 (Néo dialect, Tömotu Neo, 1972, one informant) states outright that stress may fall on any syllable of the word and treats placement as morphologically governed (accented vs unaccented articles/classifiers), whereas the existing statement of record, Boerger 2022 (Natügu, long-term fieldwork), gives fixed penultimate primary stress with foot-based secondary stress. Wurm 1969 (Malo dialect, same islet) sits between them: stress partly predictable, possibly phonemic. Boerger's description is the authoritative one, and de la Fontinelle's own cited forms (nény, møréa, dá-kæ-nǿ-ŋy, tœ-mámi) and the bulk of her stress-marked wordlist are penultimate, with only a handful of final or antepenultimate items (torô, nœl'vyn, ve'i, ma'i; 'esâmœ, 'etlomœ as scanned-read), so the conflict is best described as an older, thinner source asserting free stress on data that mostly fit the penultimate rule. Note also that the retired code [stc] spans Nalögo, for which Alfarano 2021 (held by the project under nalo1235) gives a mora-sensitive system; that is a different language after the 2009 split, not a conflict about Natügu.

sources.citation: Alfarano, Valentina. 2021. A grammar of Nalögo, an Oceanic language of Santa Cruz Island. PhD thesis, INALCO, Paris (HAL tel-03421587).
sources.note: §2.5 Stress assignment, pp. 87-90 (analysis 'very preliminary'): mora-sensitive; disyllables of two light syllables stressed on the first (/ˈna.wɜ/ 'head'), light+heavy on the heavy final (/nɒ.ˈdɵk/ 'wall', /to.ˈkoi/ 'tongs'); most trisyllables penultimate (/be.ˈte.pu/), some initial (/ˈtɵ.pu.ti/ 'cat'); affixes and clitics count for stress, prefix i- extrametrical, a heavy suffix attracts stress (/i.ˈpwɵk/). Covers the other half of the retired [stc] scope (Nalögo = S. Santa Cruz).
